Donovan Marx, 50, was attacked during a house robbery on his farm in Ventersdorp, a small town in South Africa's North West province, last Wednesday. stories.title: Africa: Strengthening Africa's Outbreak-Ready Evidence Generation Capabilities
stories.summary: Strengthening Africa's Outbreak-Ready Evidence Generation Capabilities 26 October 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Addis Ababa) 26 October 2026; OSLO; -- CEPI's Research Preparedness Program, which aims to strengthen regional clinical trial readiness and emergency evidence generation, today announced up to US$8.2 million in additional funding to the Technical Coordinating Partners leading its West Africa component -- the International Vaccine Institute (IVI) and MRC Unit The Gambia at LSHTM (MRCG) -- to support implementation of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC)'s hub-and-spoke clinical trial model. The funding, announced at a launch event on 22nd October in Accra convened by Africa CDC, African Medicines Agency, WHO AFRO and CEPI, supports Africa CDC's hub-and-spoke network which connects experienced clinical trial research "hubs" to a wider network of "spoke" sites closer to outbreak-prone areas. It is designed to enable faster, more coordinated generation of clinical evidence during epidemics and pandemics, strengthening regional readiness for future health emergencies. The initial implementation will focus on West Africa, before expanding to other regions of Africa. "Strengthening clinical trial systems before outbreaks occur, in regions where they are more common, is critical if we are to generate evidence without delay when new threats emerge," said Dr Richard Hatchett, CEPI CEO . "By supporting Africa CDC's hub-and-spoke model, we are helping to build a better connected and coordinated regional clinical research network -- fully aligned with CEPI's 3.0 Strategy, which has a key focus on strengthening globally connected research networks to accelerate outbreak response and the development of vaccines." Across Africa, multiple outbreaks of infectious diseases occur each year that rapidly spread across communities and borders--many have no approved vaccines to defend against them. The ongoing Bundibugyo ebolavirus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is a stark, current example of such.

But the mission has faced mounting pressure since a US decision to withdraw funding. Uganda announced on Monday that it had begun pulling its troops out of Somalia, where it has been a key player in efforts to counter insurgents for almost two decades. "The first cohort of troops under the phased withdrawal operation have already arrived back in Uganda," a statement from the Ugandan military said. Uganda was the first country to send troops to Somalia as part of an African Union peacekeeping force set up in 2007 to support the Somali government battling Al-Shabab Islamist militants. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Uganda "will gradually withdraw all its forces in Somalia, including those currently deployed under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) by the close of 2027," the military's statement added, referring to the latest African Union mission.

stories.title: Roy Moxham obituary
stories.summary: Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books View image in fullscreen Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books Obituary Roy Moxham obituary My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India , a country he visited many times on extended trips. His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company. Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.

stories.title: Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Yiech Pur Biel (left) is leading the first ever refugee team at the Youth Olympics By Lizzy Bella BBC Newsbeat Published 30 October 2026 When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee. "That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat. In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil. Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission. Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".

stories.title: How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, US Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald vowed to pursue all those involved By Ondiro Oganga Reporting from Nairobi Published 30 October 2026 In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents. Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system. On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft. Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges. Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.

stories.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
stories.summary: View image in fullscreen Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Wemmer Pan Road, near Rosettenville in Johannesburg, has been occupied by illegal gold miners. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian C ora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area. In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa , meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare). Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site. “We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked. Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide” .

stories.title: East Africa: CMA CGM Launches a New Dedicated Rail Service in Kenya, Strengthening Its Presence in East Africa
stories.summary: CMA CGM Launches a New Dedicated Rail Service in Kenya, Strengthening Its Presence in East Africa CMA CGM CMA CGM launches its first dedicated full block train service between the Port of Mombasa 29 October 2026 Content from a Premium Partner InfoWire CMA CGM launches its first dedicated full block train service between the Port of Mombasa and the Nairobi-Embakasi Inland Container Depot, strengthening connections between Kenya’s main maritime gateway and its inland markets. With 54 wagons and a capacity of 108 containers (Twenty-foot Equivalent Units), the service will initially operate one train per week, with potential to increase frequency and introduce a return service. Developed in partnership with the Kenya Ports Authority and Kenya Railways Corporation, the initiative strengthens CMA CGM’s logistics offering and long-term commitment to Kenya and East Africa. CMA CGM, a global player in sea, land, air and logistics solutions, launched its first dedicated full block train service between the Port of Mombasa and the Nairobi-Embakasi Inland Container Depot (ICD) on 28 October. With 54 wagons and a capacity of 108 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), the service strengthens the connection between Kenya’s main maritime gateway and its inland logistics network.

stories.title: Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws
stories.summary: Image caption, Neema Munuo, whose 18-year-old daughter Maria Chami was shot dead on the day of the election, wants the government to acknowledge her suffering By Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Dar es Salaam ,Â Basillioh Rukanga Â and Â Lucy Fleming Published 29 October 2026 Families affected by election-related violence in Tanzania that led to the deaths of at least 500 people a year ago have told the BBC they want justice for those killed in the protests and help with medical expenses for those injured. "We can no longer afford to pay hospital bills," Meshack Sane, who was shot in the leg, told the BBC. On the eve of the anniversary of the poll that saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan elected with 98% of the vote, rights group Amnesty International also accused her government of "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear". The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as Samia's two main challengers were excluded. Tundu Lissu, the 58-year-old leader of the main opposition Chadema party, had been put on trial for treason ahead of the poll - preventing him from standing. He had been demanding electoral reforms and a verdict in his case is due next week.

stories.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
stories.summary: Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, pictured in 2017. Photograph: Roger Anis/AP View image in fullscreen Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, pictured in 2017. Photograph: Roger Anis/AP Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country. Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt. According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups. “Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

stories.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
stories.summary: A map showing countries affected by active Ebola outbreaks at the headquarters of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention in Abuja. Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/Reuters View image in fullscreen A map showing countries affected by active Ebola outbreaks at the headquarters of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention in Abuja. Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/Reuters Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials. As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths , Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies. “We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment. “It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

stories.title: Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
stories.summary: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola By Basillioh Rukanga Reporting from Nairobi Published 21 October 2026 Updated 27 October 2026 As fears grow that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could spread further, Kenya, which announced its first Ebola case three weeks ago and has since had eight more cases, is hoping for the opposite. Nine cases and two deaths have so far been confirmed. With the first 20 of the people who came into contact with the first Ebola patient being released, the government has described it as a "milestone worth celebrating". The government expects the outbreak to be declared over in less than two months, if efforts to contain the spread holds. But that is assuming there are no more cases, including from the 98 people still in quarantine and due to be freed next week.
